flags.detail: Key A ("B") is correct and verified — I compiled the exact program with g++ 13.3 -std=c++17 and it printed B. The defect is the last clause of the explanation: "it would only become undefined if speak() were pure virtual with no definition, since there would then be no function to call." That states the UB condition more narrowly than the standard does. [class.abstract]/6 says the effect of making a *virtual call* to a pure virtual function, directly or indirectly, for the object being constructed or destroyed from a constructor or destructor is undefined — full stop, with no carve-out for a pure virtual that happens to have a definition. I verified the corner case: with `struct B { B(){ speak(); } virtual void speak() = 0; }; void B::speak(){ ... }` g++ compiles it, warns "pure virtual 'virtual void B::speak()' called from constructor", and at run time happens to print the base definition and exit 0 — i.e. this is UB that a real compiler makes look benign, which is exactly the shape of error the explanation would teach a reader to trust. (What *is* well defined is a qualified, non-virtual call such as `B::speak();` from the constructor, which I also compiled and ran.) Fix: replace the clause with something like "it would become undefined if speak() were pure virtual, since a virtual call to a pure virtual function from a constructor or destructor is undefined whether or not the base supplies a definition; only a qualified call such as B::speak() is safe there."
flags.suggested: A (key unchanged); rewrite the final sentence of the explanation as described.

flags.detail: Key A is correct: I compiled `fstream f("rec.dat", ios::out | ios::binary)` against a pre-existing 16-byte rec.dat and re-checked the size immediately after the open — it was 0, confirming `out` with neither `in` nor `app` maps to stdio "w" and truncates at open. The problem is the explanation's closing clause, "which is also why the seek to a later record could not find anything." That is not what happens. In the same test, `f.seekp(4, ios::beg)` on the now-empty file succeeded: fail() was false and tellp() reported 4. The subsequent 4-byte write produced an 8-byte file consisting of four NUL bytes followed by the record (verified with od -c). So seeking past end-of-file on an output file stream is legal and succeeds; it creates a gap on write rather than failing. As written the explanation could teach that a seek beyond EOF is an error, and it also slightly overstates the stem's premise (the file does not end up holding only the one record — it holds the zero-fill up to the seek offset plus the record). Fix: drop or replace that clause, e.g. "...the records were destroyed at open; the later seek still succeeds, and the write simply lands past a zero-filled gap in an otherwise empty file."
flags.suggested: A (key unchanged); delete the "the seek to a later record could not find anything" clause.

flags.detail: Key B (std::length_error) is correct — I verified the whole hierarchy with std::is_base_of at compile time: length_error, out_of_range, domain_error and invalid_argument are logic_error; range_error, overflow_error, underflow_error and system_error are runtime_error. The wrong specific is the header attribution in the stem: it asks about "the standard exception hierarchy of <stdexcept>" but offers std::system_error as option D, and std::system_error is declared in <system_error>, not <stdexcept>. Verified: a TU that includes only <stdexcept> and names std::system_error fails with "'system_error' in namespace 'std' does not name a type" under g++ 13.3. The explanation repeats the error by grouping "std::overflow_error and std::system_error" as though both belonged to the same header's hierarchy. The key is unaffected, but a candidate revising header contents is taught something false, and strictly a reader who knows system_error is not in <stdexcept> has to decide whether the stem excludes it from consideration at all. Fix: swap option D for std::underflow_error, which is a genuine <stdexcept> runtime_error descendant and an equally good distractor, or drop the "<stdexcept>" framing from the stem and say "the standard exception hierarchy".
flags.suggested: B (key unchanged); replace option D "std::system_error" with "std::underflow_error".

notes: All 34 questions reviewed; 3 flags, none of which changes a keyed letter — every key in this half is correct. I compiled and ran 24 test programs with g++ 13.3 -std=c++17, confirming among others: 042 prints D1 (dynamic dispatch with static default argument), 043 prints B, 041 is an ambiguous-reference compile error and virtual inheritance fixes it, 048 fails as abstract because of the missing const, 051 prints 4, 052's seekg is ignored while failbit is set (tellg returned -1; note it does clear eofbit first, which neither the option nor the explanation misstates), 053 truncates at open, 055 gcount() is 40, 056's option C does not compile on an ifstream, 059 prints ***427, 060 prints acX, 061's throw e; slices out_of_range to exception while a bare throw; does not, 062 and 064 both call std::terminate with the intervening destructor never running, 067's c_str() pointer is genuinely invalidated by the append, and 050's key-function omission does produce 'undefined reference to vtable for Widget'. The three flags are all explanation-level: a UB condition stated too narrowly (043), a verified-false claim about a seek past EOF (053), and a header misattribution for std::system_error (063). I attacked but did not flag 037's "number of operands cannot be altered" (std::operator() has variable arity, but the grammar does not fix it either, so the claim survives) or 053's mild imprecision about the resulting file size beyond the clause noted.
